list.listitem: Epicondylitis is inflammation of the bony origin of the wrist extensors (lateral or tennis elbow) or wrist flexors (medial or golfer's elbow), usually from repetitive use.

Indications for procedure include: Persistent symptoms despite change in activity, rest, anti-inflammatory medication, counterforce bracing and physical therapy is the usual indication epicondyle injection. Severe symptoms causing significant pain and dysfunction unresponsive to conservative management. Desire for rapid return of function.

Note: Improvement after corticosteroid injection may be short lived as there is no evidence for long-term benefit when compared with other therapies for lateral epicondylitis. One RCT of 198 patients found better short-term outcomes with injection, but better long-term outcomes in those randomized to physical therapy.A systematic review concluded that the overall quality of studies of injection was poor and provided no firm conclusions to guide practice.

A Cochrane review, based on moderate-certainty evidence, found minimal or no benefit from autologous blood and platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection therapy for lateral elbow pain or tennis elbow. Given the cost and risks (e.g., pain, infection), the authors concluded that their use was not warranted.
Local infection over or near the epicondyle
Possible fracture (exclude with appropriate diagnostic imaging)
Lack of response to two or more previous injections
Allergy to local anesthetics or injectable corticosteroids
Sterile gloves
Bactericidal solution for skin preparation: povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine
Fenestrated sterile drape
Ethyl chloride topical refrigerant (optional)
4 x 4 gauze pads
Syringe (10 cc) and needles (21 gauge for drawing medication and 25 or 27 gauge for injection)
Lidocaine, 1% plain (2-3 cc total dose)
Injectable corticosteroid of choice (10-20 mg methylprednisolone or equivalent)
Adhesive bandage or other dressing
Obtain informed consent.
Position patient to obtain best access to epicondyle with arm at side and elbow flexed at 45°. For medial epicondyle, wrist pronated (). For lateral epicondyle, hand supinated ().
Mark site of maximal pain with pen (optional), and preparation desired site with bactericidal solution and sterile drape.

Palpate the point of maximal tenderness usually found just distal to the medial/lateral epicondyle. Then, spray site with topical skin refrigerant, ie, ethyl chloride, immediately before injection (optional).
Using sterile technique, insert 25 or 27 gauge at 90° into site of maximal pain with 2 to 3 cc lidocaine and 10 to 20 mg methylprednisolone in a 10 cc syringe.
Complete injection before withdrawing needle to avoid SC corticosteroid deposition.
Apply dressing such as an adhesive bandage.
Patient remains in supine position for 1 to 2 minutes after injection to assess for potential vasovagal response, then slowly sit up.
Monitor patient for adverse reactions to the injection such as drug reaction for 30 minutes after the procedure.
SC corticosteroid infiltration can cause fat atrophy and skin depigmentation. This can be avoided by completing the injection before withdrawing the needle.
Steroid flare occurs in 25% of patients within 48 hours at site of corticosteroid injection. Warn patients and treat with ice, rest, and anti-inflammatory medication.
Bleeding usually responds to direct pressure.
Infection is rare, but warning signs should be given to patient. Antibiotics to cover common skin flora are appropriate if infection occurs, but not prophylactically.
No routine follow-up is necessary unless symptoms fail to improve, then patient can return in 2 to 3 weeks for reassessment.
Consider repeat corticosteroid injection in 6 to 8 weeks.

Consider referral to physical therapy. A Cochrane review found low-certainty evidence that manual therapy and prescribed exercises may provide modest improvement in pain and disability in the short-term (ie, up to 3 months).
CPT: 20550 Injection: tendon sheath, ligament, trigger point or ganglion.
Typical fees for this procedure: $45 to $100.
Time off work varies depending on patient's normal daily activities. Advise patient not to do heavy lifting or repetitive activity for 48 to 72 hours after injection.
Nursing considerations: None.
